title: The Max Di-Cut approximation threshold to accuracy 1/100 under Unique Games
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal:
Assuming the Unique Games Conjecture and \(\mathsf{NP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}\), determine the optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio \(\alpha_{\rm DC}\) for Max Di-Cut with certified absolute error at most \(1/100\). Equivalently, supply a real number \(q\) and prove under these assumptions that
\[
|q-\alpha_{\rm DC}|\le1/100.
\]
The finite weighted graph model, randomized ratio convention and both assumptions are defined below. The requested accuracy is a known conditional target; the exact optimal ratio is not asserted to be known.
why: Max Di-Cut is a standard directed constraint-satisfaction problem whose approximation threshold differs from that of undirected Max Cut. Its precise ratio remains interesting, but the benchmark’s one-hundredth numerical tolerance is already covered by a much tighter published interval.

sentences: Max Di-Cut maximizes the total weight of directed edges leaving a chosen side of a partition.
The numerical target is the best ratio achievable by randomized polynomial-time algorithms.
The selected assumptions are Unique Games and NP not contained in BPP.
Published bounds place the ratio between 0.87446 and 0.87461, already much more precise than one hundredth.
The record is archived for that known conditional accuracy, while exact determination remains a stronger question.

definitions:
An instance is a finite directed graph on \([n]\), given by an explicit list of ordered pairs of distinct vertices and their nonnegative rational weights in binary. Oppositely directed edges and repeated edges are allowed; repeated edges can equivalently be merged by adding their weights. A cut is a set \(S\subseteq[n]\), encoded by its characteristic bit vector, with value
\[
\operatorname{val}(S)=\sum_{(u,v):u\in S,\ v\notin S}w_{uv},\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}=\max_{S\subseteq[n]}\operatorname{val}(S).
\]
Only edges leaving \(S\) count. All vertices are listed explicitly so that output length is polynomial in the input length \(L\). Zero total edge weight is allowed and makes every cut optimal. This is the rational weighted Max Di-Cut convention used by the cited theorem; unit-weight graphs are included.

A rational \(r\in[0,1]\) is achievable if one uniform randomized multitape Turing machine, with constants \(K,b\), returns a cut on every execution within \(K(L+2)^b\) bit steps and, on every instance, returns a cut of value at least \(r\operatorname{OPT}\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Random bits are independent fair bits; their generation, finite-precision arithmetic and output are charged. There is no real-arithmetic oracle, advice or free preprocessing. The program and constants may depend on \(r\). Define \(\alpha_{\rm DC}\) as the supremum of the achievable rational ratios. It lies in \([0,1]\); the supremum need not itself be achieved.

For the Unique Games Conjecture, a finite instance has a graph, a fixed alphabet \([s]\), nonnegative rational edge weights summing to one and, for each oriented edge \((u,v)\), a permutation \(\pi_{uv}\) of \([s]\), with the reverse permutation its inverse. A labeling \(a:V\to[s]\) satisfies an edge if \(a(v)=\pi_{uv}(a(u))\); its value is the total satisfied weight. Let \(\operatorname{UGval}\) be the maximum value over labelings. The conjecture says that for every pair of positive rational constants \(\eta,\zeta\) with \(\eta+\zeta<1\), some fixed \(s\ge2\) makes distinguishing \(\operatorname{UGval}\ge1-\eta\) from \(\operatorname{UGval}\le\zeta\) NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. Concretely, there must be a polynomial-time reduction from Boolean 3-CNF satisfiability preserving these yes and no cases.

The additional assumption \(\mathsf{NP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}\) means that not every language with polynomial-length, polynomial-time verifiable witnesses has a uniform randomized polynomial-time decision algorithm with error at most \(1/3\) on each input. Equivalently here, Boolean 3-CNF satisfiability has no such algorithm. It is stated separately because a UG-hardness reduction alone does not rule out randomized algorithms if all NP problems were in BPP.

A valid numerical answer may be a rational, a rigorously specified real expression, or an enclosing interval \([\ell,u]\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\), whose midpoint has the requested error. No time limit is imposed on finding the answer or its certificate. Both bounds must concern the optimal ratio over all algorithms in the given model, rather than just one SDP rounding family. Merely naming the defining supremum again does not give a numerical answer.
answer_criterion: Supply a concrete numerical approximation and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of absolute error at most 1/100 under the two stated assumptions, or a Lean-checked enclosing interval of width at most 1/50. Justify both the algorithmic lower bound and the conditional upper bound. This archived record does not request an exact threshold or claim that a Lean formalization of the cited proof has already been completed.

context_blocks.text: The problem page itself records an interval far narrower than one hundredth, while asking for the exact best ratio. The archival decision concerns the selected numerical tolerance, not exact determination.

The checked theorems give \(0.87446\le\alpha_{\rm DC}\le0.87461\) under the stated assumptions. Their midpoint \(q=174907/200000=0.874535\) has certified error at most \(15/200000=0.000075<1/100\). Thus the requested conditional accuracy is already known.

The upper bound follows from UG-hardness, not a restriction on a particular algorithm design. The lower bound uses a distribution of rounding rules certified by interval arithmetic, together with a small probability of independent rounding to handle low-completeness configurations. This review checked the theorem statements and that final combination, without claiming an independent rerun of the computer-assisted certificate.

The theorem’s expected-value algorithm gives the same supremum under the per-input probability convention: for any fixed positive slack, bounded output value turns an expectation guarantee into a positive constant success probability, and independent repetition boosts it. Finite precision can be absorbed into that slack. Taking the supremum removes the arbitrarily small loss.
